Don't fix production code yourself; if you find a spec violation or crash, report the failing items (file:line, spec line, repro) in your REPORT so I can route them — do not send verdicts to builders directly. Do not review builder code style; only spec compliance/crashes.

## What NOT to save in memory

- Code patterns, conventions, architecture, file paths, or project structure — these can be derived by reading the current project state.
- Git history, recent changes, or who-changed-what — `git log` / `git blame` are authoritative.
- Debugging solutions or fix recipes — the fix is in the code; the commit message has the context.
- Anything already documented in CLAUDE.md files.
- Ephemeral task details: in-progress work, temporary state, current conversation context.

These exclusions apply even when the user explicitly asks you to save. If they ask you to save a PR list or activity summary, ask what was *surprising* or *non-obvious* about it — that is the part worth keeping.

## How to save memories

Saving a memory is a two-step process:

**Step 1** — write the memory to its own file (e.g., `user_role.md`, `feedback_testing.md`) using this frontmatter format:

```markdown
---
name: {{short-kebab-case-slug}}
description: {{one-line summary, used to decide relevance in future conversations, so be specific}}
metadata:
  type: {{user, feedback, project, reference}}
---

{{memory content — for feedback/project types, structure as: rule/fact, then **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Link related memories with [[their-name]].}}
```

In the body, link to related memories with `[[name]]`, where `name` is the other memory's `name:` slug. Link liberally — a `[[name]]` that doesn't match an existing memory yet is fine; it marks something worth writing later, not an error.

**Step 2** — add a pointer to that file in `MEMORY.md`. `MEMORY.md` is an index, not a memory — each entry should be one line, under ~150 characters: `- [Title](file.md) — one-line hook`. It has no frontmatter. Never write memory content directly into `MEMORY.md`.

- `MEMORY.md` is always loaded into your conversation context — lines after 200 will be truncated, so keep the index concise
- Keep the name, description, and type fields in memory files up-to-date with the content
- Organize memory semantically by topic, not chronologically
- Update or remove memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated
- Do not write duplicate memories. First check if there is an existing memory you can update before writing a new one.

## When to access memories
- When memories seem relevant, or the user references prior-conversation work.
- You MUST access memory when the user explicitly asks you to check, recall, or remember.
- If the user says to *ignore* or *not use* memory: Do not apply remembered facts, cite, compare against, or mention memory content.
- Memory records can become stale over time. Use memory as context for what was true at a given point in time. Before answering the user or building assumptions based solely on information in memory records, verify that the memory is still correct and up-to-date by reading the current state of the files or resources. If a recalled memory conflicts with current information, trust what you observe now — and update or remove the stale memory rather than acting on it.

## Before recommending from memory

A memory that names a specific function, file, or flag is a claim that it existed *when the memory was written*. It may have been renamed, removed, or never merged. Before recommending it:

- If the memory names a file path: check the file exists.
- If the memory names a function or flag: grep for it.
- If the user is about to act on your recommendation (not just asking about history), verify first.

"The memory says X exists" is not the same as "X exists now."

A memory that summarizes repo state (activity logs, architecture snapshots) is frozen in time. If the user asks about *recent* or *current* state, prefer `git log` or reading the code over recalling the snapshot.

## Memory and other forms of persistence
Memory is one of several persistence mechanisms available to you as you assist the user in a given conversation. The distinction is often that memory can be recalled in future conversations and should not be used for persisting information that is only useful within the scope of the current conversation.
- When to use or update a plan instead of memory: If you are about to start a non-trivial implementation task and would like to reach alignment with the user on your approach you should use a Plan rather than saving this information to memory. Similarly, if you already have a plan within the conversation and you have changed your approach persist that change by updating the plan rather than saving a memory.
- When to use or update tasks instead of memory: When you need to break your work in current conversation into discrete steps or keep track of your progress use tasks instead of saving to memory. Tasks are great for persisting information about the work that needs to be done in the current conversation, but memory should be reserved for information that will be useful in future conversations.

- Since this memory is local-scope (not checked into version control), tailor your memories to this project and machine

content.content: # Meeting-room booking app — full spec (verbatim from the user; final, no questions allowed) Constraints: Use only Node.js built-ins (no npm install). Node v22. Do not use the Fable model. Build a meeting-room booking app: an HTTP server `server.mjs` (an ES module, run as `node server.mjs`) that serves a JSON API and a browser page, and keeps its data in one JSON file. ## Server - At startup the server checks `PORT`, then reads the data file, then starts listening, in that order. - It listens on 127.0.0.1 at the port in the `PORT` environment variable. An unset or empty `PORT` means 3000. A `PORT` that is not made only of ASCII digits 0-9, or whose value is above 65535, or a port that cannot be bound (for example because it is in use), makes the server write one line of its choice to stderr and exit with code 1. - Once listening, it prints `listening on http://127.0.0.1:` followed by "\n" to stdout, where `` is the port actually bound (with `PORT=0`, the port the OS picked). This line is the only thing the server ever writes to stdout. - Its data lives in the file named by the `DATA_FILE` environment variable, as JSON in a layout of your choice. An unset or empty `DATA_FILE` means `bookings.json`. A relative `DATA_FILE`, the default included, is resolved against the current working directory, not the folder of `server.mjs`. - The server reads the data file once, at startup. If reading it fails with `ENOENT` (the file, or a folder on its path, does not exist), there are no bookings yet. If reading it fails in any other way (for example the path is a directory), or its content is not data in the layout this server writes (for example it is empty or not valid JSON), the server writes `cannot read data file ` followed by "\n" to stderr, where `` is the value of `DATA_FILE` as given (`bookings.json` when it is unset or empty), and exits with code 1 without listening. - After startup the server's memory is the truth: changes made to the file from outside are not noticed. The server writes the data file only when a POST creates a booking or a DELETE removes one, never at startup or for any other request, and it never creates folders. - Every change is saved to the data file before its reply is sent: after a restart with the same `DATA_FILE`, the bookings, and the id the next booking will get, are as before. - If saving a change fails (for example because the data file's folder does not exist), the reply is 500 `internal error` and nothing changes, the next id included. Any other unexpected failure while handling a request also replies 500 `internal error`. In both cases the server keeps running. - Requests that arrive at the same time give the same result as if they had been handled one at a time in some order: of several overlapping bookings sent at once while saving works, exactly one is created and every other one gets 409, and no id is given twice. - Before sending any reply, the server reads the whole request body, if there is one, and discards what it does not use, so the client always receives the reply, the 413 and 415 replies included. ## API - The rooms are fixed: `Aurora`, `Borealis` and `Cosmos`, in that order. - A booking is a JSON object with exactly the keys `id`, `room`, `title`, `date`, `start` and `end`: `id` is a number, the others are strings. The first booking gets id 1 and each new booking the next integer; an id is never reused, even after deletes and restarts. - Only the parsed JSON of a reply body matters: whitespace and key order in it are free. - A request's path is its request target up to the first `?` (all of it when there is no `?`). Routes compare the path byte for byte, with no percent-decoding and no dot-segment, slash or letter-case normalisation: `/api/%62ookings`, `/api/./rooms`, `/API/rooms` and `/api/bookings/` are none of the paths below. The query, the text after the first `?`, is ignored unless stated, and is decoded as `new URLSearchParams(query)` does. - `GET /api/rooms`: 200 `{"rooms": ["Aurora", "Borealis", "Cosmos"]}`. - `GET /api/bookings`: 200 `{"bookings": [...]}` with every booking, sorted by date, then start, then room in the order above. When the query has a `date` parameter (as `params.has('date')` says; `?date` with no `=` counts, with the empty value), its value is `params.get('date')` (the first one when repeated) and the reply holds only the bookings on that date; a value that is not a valid date by rule 6 below (the empty value included) gets 400 `date must be a valid YYYY-MM-DD date`. Other query parameters are ignored. - `POST /api/bookings` with a JSON body holding `room`, `title`, `date`, `start` and `end`: 201 and the new booking. Other keys in the body are ignored. - `DELETE /api/bookings/`: every path that is `/api/bookings/` followed by a non-empty `` holding no `/` is this route, whatever `` is. The reply is 204 with an empty body, and the booking is gone. When `` is not a positive integer written in ASCII digits 0-9 without a leading zero, or no booking has that id: 404 `booking not found`. - `GET /` and `GET /app.js` serve the page (see Page). - Any other path: 404 `not found`, whatever the method. This includes every path that starts with `/api/bookings/` and whose rest is empty or holds a `/`, such as `/api/bookings/` and `/api/bookings/1/`. - A path above with a method not listed for it (HEAD and OPTIONS included): 405 `method not allowed`. For example `GET /api/bookings/abc` is 405. A 405 reply may or may not have an `Allow` header; it is not checked. - Every reply with a body other than the page and the script has `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8`. An error reply is `{"error": ""}` with exactly that key, where `` is the text given here. ## Booking rules (`POST /api/bookings`; the first rule that fails decides the reply) 1. The media type of the `Content-Type` header (the part before the first `;`, with spaces and tabs removed from both ends, letter case ignored) is not `application/json`, or the header is missing: 415 `content type must be application/json`. 2. The body is longer than 10000 bytes, counting the body bytes actually received: 413 `body too large`. 3. The body, decoded as `Buffer.prototype.toString('utf8')` does and then given to `JSON.parse`, is not a JSON object (it is empty, not valid JSON, `null`, an array, a string, a number or a boolean): 400 `body must be a JSON object`. Bytes that are not valid UTF-8 become U+FFFD and are not an error by themselves. A byte order mark at the very start is kept, so such a body is not valid JSON. 4. `room` is not a string equal to one of the room names (letter case matters): 400 `room must be one of Aurora, Borealis, Cosmos`. 5. `title` is not a string, or is shorter than 1 or longer than 80 UTF-16 code units after removing the whitespace at both ends (as `String.prototype.trim` does): 400 `title must be 1 to 80 characters`. The booking keeps the trimmed title. 6. `date` is not a string `YYYY-MM-DD` (4, 2 and 2 ASCII digits 0-9) naming a real day from 2000-01-01 to 2099-12-31, where February has 29 days in years divisible by 4: 400 `date must be a valid YYYY-MM-DD date`. 7. `start` is not a string `HH:MM` (2 and 2 ASCII digits 0-9) from `00:00` to `23:59`: 400 `start must be HH:MM`. 8. `end` is not such a string: 400 `end must be HH:MM`. 9. `end` is not later than `start`: 400 `end must be after start`. 10. The booking overlaps a booking of the same room on the same date, that is each of the two starts before the other ends (a booking may start exactly when another ends): 409 `room is already booked from to `, with the start and end of the overlapping booking that starts earliest. - No field except `title` is trimmed or changed: ` 2026-11-03`, `2026-11-3` and `9:00` are invalid. ## Page - `GET /` answers 200 with `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8` and the page. `GET /app.js` answers 200 with `Content-Type: text/javascript; charset=utf-8` and the page's script. - The page loads the script with a `

1	# Room bookings
2	
3	A small meeting-room booking app. One Node.js file (`server.mjs`) serves a
4	JSON API and a browser page, and keeps every booking in a single JSON file.
5	
6	There are three fixed rooms: `Aurora`, `Borealis` and `Cosmos`.
7	
8	## Requirements
9	
10	- Node.js 22 or later.
11	- No dependencies. The app uses only Node.js built-ins, so there is nothing to
12	  `npm install`.
13	
14	## Running the server
15	
16	```sh
17	npm start
18	# or
19	node server.mjs
20	```
21	
22	The server listens on `127.0.0.1` only. Once it is listening it prints one
23	line to stdout:
24	
25	```
26	listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000
27	```
28	
29	### Environment variables
30	
31	| Variable    | Default         | Meaning |
32	|-------------|-----------------|---------|
33	| `PORT`      | `3000`          | Port to listen on. Must be ASCII digits only and at most 65535. `0` lets the OS choose a free port; the printed line shows the port actually bound. |
34	| `DATA_FILE` | `bookings.json` | Path of the data file. A relative path is resolved against the current working directory, not the folder of `server.mjs`. |
35	
36	An unset or empty variable uses its default.
37	
38	Examples:
39	
40	```sh
41	PORT=8080 node server.mjs
42	PORT=0 node server.mjs                      # OS picks the port
43	DATA_FILE=/var/data/rooms.json npm start
44	DATA_FILE=data/bookings.json PORT=4000 npm start
45	```
46	
47	### Startup and exit codes
48	
49	At startup the server checks `PORT`, then reads the data file, then starts
50	listening. It exits with code 1, after writing one line to stderr, when:
51	
52	- `PORT` is not made only of digits, is above 65535, or cannot be bound
53	  (for example because it is already in use);
54	- the data file cannot be read for any reason other than "does not exist"
55	  (for example the path is a directory), or its content is not valid data
56	  (for example empty or not JSON). The message is then
57	  `cannot read data file <name>`, where `<name>` is `DATA_FILE` as given.
58	
59	A data file that does not exist (or whose folder does not exist) simply means
60	there are no bookings yet.
61	
62	### The data file
63	
64	The data file is UTF-8 JSON managed by the server. It holds the id the next
65	booking will get and the list of bookings:
66	
67	```json
68	{
69	  "nextId": 3,
70	  "bookings": [
71	    { "id": 2, "room": "Aurora", "title": "Standup", "date": "2026-11-03", "start": "09:00", "end": "10:00" }
72	  ]
73	}
74	```
75	
76	At startup the server checks the content strictly. The top level must have
77	exactly the keys `nextId` (an integer, at least 1) and `bookings` (an array).
78	Each booking must have exactly the six booking keys and follow the booking
79	rules: a known room, a trimmed title of 1 to 80 characters, a valid date and
80	times, and `start` before `end`. Each id must be unique and below `nextId`,
81	and no two bookings may overlap. Anything else, including an empty file,
82	invalid JSON or a byte order mark, stops startup with
83	`cannot read data file <name>`. To start with an empty store, delete the file
84	or write `{"nextId":1,"bookings":[]}`.
85	
86	Keep these points in mind:
87	
88	- It is read once, at startup. Changes made to it from outside while the
89	  server runs are not noticed.
90	- It is written only when a booking is created or deleted, and each change is
91	  saved before the reply is sent. After a restart with the same `DATA_FILE`,
92	  the bookings and the next booking id are the same as before.
93	- A save writes a temporary file `<DATA_FILE>.<pid>.tmp` next to the data
94	  file and then renames it over the data file. An interrupted save therefore
95	  never leaves a half-written data file.
96	- The server never creates folders. If saving fails (for example the folder
97	  does not exist), the request gets `500 internal error`, nothing changes, and
98	  the server keeps running.
99	
100	## The browser page
101	
102	Open `http://127.0.0.1:3000/` (or whichever port you chose). The page has:
103	
104	- a form (Room, Title, Date, Start, End, then **Book**) that creates a booking;
105	- a booking list, with a **Cancel** button next to each booking;
106	- a **Show date** filter that shows only the bookings on one date, and a
107	  **Show all** button that clears it;
108	- an error line that shows the server's error message, or
109	  `Could not reach the server.` when there is no reply. If a reply has an
110	  unexpected shape, it shows `Request failed.` instead.
111	
112	The page itself does no validation: every check is made by the server, and
113	its error message is shown as is. The page loads its script from `/app.js`.
114	
115	## API
116	
117	All paths are matched exactly, byte for byte: no percent-decoding, no
118	case folding, no trailing-slash or dot-segment normalisation. The query
119	string is ignored unless a route says otherwise.
120	
121	Every JSON reply has `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8`. An
122	error reply is always:
123	
124	```json
125	{ "error": "<message>" }
126	```
127	
128	### Bookings
129	
130	A booking is a JSON object with exactly these keys:
131	
132	```json
133	{
134	  "id": 1,
135	  "room": "Aurora",
136	  "title": "Standup",
137	  "date": "2026-11-03",
138	  "start": "09:00",
139	  "end": "10:00"
140	}
141	```
142	
143	`id` is a number; the other fields are strings. The first booking gets id 1
144	and every new booking the next integer. Ids are never reused, even after
145	deletes and restarts.
146	
147	### Routes
148	
149	| Method   | Path                  | Success |
150	|----------|-----------------------|---------|
151	| `GET`    | `/api/rooms`          | `200 {"rooms": ["Aurora", "Borealis", "Cosmos"]}` |
152	| `GET`    | `/api/bookings`       | `200 {"bookings": [...]}` |
153	| `POST`   | `/api/bookings`       | `201` with the new booking |
154	| `DELETE` | `/api/bookings/<id>`  | `204` with an empty body |
155	| `GET`    | `/`                   | `200` the page (`text/html; charset=utf-8`) |
156	| `GET`    | `/app.js`             | `200` the page script (`text/javascript; charset=utf-8`) |
157	
158	#### `GET /api/bookings`
159	
160	Returns every booking, sorted by date, then start time, then room (in the
161	order Aurora, Borealis, Cosmos).
162	
163	With a `date` query parameter, only the bookings on that date are returned.
164	`?date` with no value counts as the empty value; when `date` is repeated, the
165	first one is used. Other query parameters are ignored.
166	
167	- `400 date must be a valid YYYY-MM-DD date` when the `date` value is not a
168	  valid date (see rule 6 below), the empty value included.
169	
170	#### `POST /api/bookings`
171	
172	Send `Content-Type: application/json` and a JSON object with `room`, `title`,
173	`date`, `start` and `end`. Other keys are ignored. The reply is `201` and the
174	new booking.
175	
176	#### `DELETE /api/bookings/<id>`
177	
178	Deletes the booking. Any path of the form `/api/bookings/<id>`, where `<id>`
179	is non-empty and holds no `/`, is this route.
180	
181	- `404 booking not found` when `<id>` is not a positive integer written in
182	  digits without a leading zero (for example `abc`, `0`, `01`), or no booking
183	  has that id.
184	
185	### Booking rules
186	
187	`POST /api/bookings` checks these rules in order; the first one that fails
188	decides the reply.
189	
190	| # | Rule | Reply |
191	|---|------|-------|
192	| 1 | The `Content-Type` media type (before any `;`, case-insensitive) must be `application/json` | `415 content type must be application/json` |
193	| 2 | The body must be at most 10000 bytes | `413 body too large` |
194	| 3 | The body must be a JSON object (not empty, invalid JSON, `null`, an array, a string, a number or a boolean) | `400 body must be a JSON object` |
195	| 4 | `room` must be exactly `Aurora`, `Borealis` or `Cosmos` (case matters) | `400 room must be one of Aurora, Borealis, Cosmos` |
196	| 5 | `title` must be a string of 1 to 80 characters after trimming whitespace at both ends | `400 title must be 1 to 80 characters` |
197	| 6 | `date` must be `YYYY-MM-DD`, a real day from 2000-01-01 to 2099-12-31 | `400 date must be a valid YYYY-MM-DD date` |
198	| 7 | `start` must be `HH:MM`, from `00:00` to `23:59` | `400 start must be HH:MM` |
199	| 8 | `end` must be `HH:MM`, from `00:00` to `23:59` | `400 end must be HH:MM` |
200	| 9 | `end` must be later than `start` | `400 end must be after start` |
201	| 10 | The booking must not overlap another booking of the same room on the same date | `409 room is already booked from <start> to <end>` |
202	
203	Notes:
204
